pre_existing_structural_split.verdict: FAIL-OPEN: every row went to train, val and test are empty, and the leakage analyzer reported 0 families and 0 leakage. A check that reports 'no leakage' for a split with no test set is not a weak check, it is a green result produced by nothing having been tested.

representation_finding.what_it_means: The tokenizer emits ONE distinct sequence per family and it does not vary with problem_size or launch_config. So 264 measured rows collapse to 8 distinct model inputs. A row-level split therefore puts token-identical examples on both sides, and a model asked to predict runtime from this representation cannot see the two things that determine runtime. This is a gpu-sim-u2o.8 finding that only became visible once the split was run on real data.

leakage_audit.note: kernel_hash is distinct on every row, so a leakage check keyed on kernel_hash reports 0% leakage on a split that leaks every row. The model never sees kernel_hash; it sees the token sequence. Keying the check on the wrong identifier is how the pre-existing analyzer returned leakage_train_test: 0.

recommended_split.rule: families sorted alphabetically; first 2 to test, next 1 to val. A stated rule rather than a random draw, so the split is reproducible and auditable instead of lucky.

size_range_holdout.why: the dataset has 4 problem sizes ([4096, 16384, 65536, 262144]) and every one of the 264 rows is measured_regime='launch_bound'. A size-range holdout needs sizes spanning more than one regime; here every size is launch-bound (7.1's finding), so holding out a size range would hold out a regime change that does not exist in the data. Recorded as impossible rather than implemented and reported as if it worked.
